# Crisis Response & Reputation Recovery — Operating Strategy
## Version 4 (revised following review)

**Document type:** Operating playbook. Part A is intended to be usable in the first hour without being read in full.
**Prepared by:** International Brand Risk working group, with the market team
**Circulated to:** Regional President (market) · Market General Manager · Group Chief Marketing Officer · Group General Counsel · Group Communications · Group Head of Security · Group Finance / Investor Relations · Group HR · Group Internal Audit
**Status:** A proposal for endorsement, offered with respect. Colleagues closer to the market, and colleagues with legal and financial responsibility, will see things the working group cannot. Where this document is wrong, we would be grateful to be corrected before it is needed rather than during.
**Figures marked *illustrative*** are placeholders to be confirmed with Finance and the market team; they are included so that the shape of the commitment is visible, not because we have any confidence in the numbers.

---

## 0. Note on this revision

The previous draft was reviewed and found, quite rightly, to be an essay rather than an instrument. We are grateful for the correction. Six things have changed, and we record them here so that colleagues who commented can see their guidance reflected:

1. The response now has **three settings, not one**. Unconditional maximum response was itself a risk; a national on-camera apology delivered against a few hundred coordinated accounts manufactures the crisis it was meant to answer.
2. **Global withdrawal is now a decision rule, not an instruction.** The earlier circularity — withdrawing globally to prevent contagion, when the withdrawal itself is the contagion vector — has been removed.
3. The **legal posture has been rewritten**. The recommendation to publish individual approval accountability has been withdrawn entirely. We publish the failure of *process*; we never publish *people*. Where our first draft treated legal exposure as generally overstated, we accept that in markets with religious-insult, national-symbol or criminal-defamation regimes the exposure falls personally on the local country manager, and that this is not ours to accept on his or her behalf.
4. **Safety, welfare and spokesperson protection** have been added. Their absence was a straightforward failure of care, and the working group regrets it.
5. A **commercial section** now exists — cost envelope, insurance notification, agency indemnity, investor materiality test.
6. The **five internal tensions** identified in review are reconciled in §17 rather than left to be argued in the room at hour three.

The diagnosis that the reviewer was kind about has been compressed and moved to Annex A. It matters, but not in the first hour.

---

# PART A — THE FIRST 72 HOURS

## 1. Action grid

Owners are given by role. **Default names should be entered before this document is filed**, and confirmed by the Regional President; an unnamed owner is an unowned action. Times are from **T0 = the moment the market team judges the reaction to be more than routine comment**, not from the moment senior management is informed.

| By | Action | Owner (R) | Consulted / Informed |
|---|---|---|---|
| T+30 min | Open incident log (single timestamped file, assume it will be disclosed one day). Convene pod on standing bridge. | Market Comms Lead | Pod |
| T+1 hr | **Freeze**: suspend all scheduled in-market activity — paid, organic, promotional, influencer, executive appearances, launches. Reversible, requires no approval. | Market Marketing Director | Media agency, Group CMO (informed) |
| T+1 hr | Notify Group Comms, Group GC, Regional President by pre-agreed one-page alert (Annex D template). No analysis, no reassurance. | Market GM | Group |
| T+2 hrs | Preliminary **safety assessment** (§6): offices, stores, distribution points, community managers, agency staff. | Group Security, with Market HR | Market GM |
| T+3 hrs | Instruct **local cultural counsel** (external, retained in advance where possible) and independent local research partner. | Market GM | Pod |
| T+4 hrs | Community managers switched to holding protocol: acknowledge, do not argue, never mock, do not mass-delete, escalate threats. | Digital / Community Lead | Market Comms Lead |
| T+6 hrs | **Reaction verification read** (§5): unique authors vs. reposts, geographic concentration, authenticity indicators, political or competitive sponsorship. First tier assignment. | Insights / Social Listening Lead | Pod decides tier |
| T+6 hrs | Legal exposure screen: statutory, criminal, regulatory, personal-liability. Written, specific, one page. | Market Counsel + Group GC | Pod |
| T+8 hrs | Brief customer service, store and call-centre staff. Permission to say "we got this wrong" without a script. Abuse-reporting route opened. | Market Customer Service Lead | Market HR |
| T+8 hrs | Direct contact — voice, not mailshot — with top retail, distribution and franchise partners. | Market Sales Director | Market GM |
| T+10 hrs | Internal note to all market employees, written as if it will be external, because it will be. | Market GM + Market HR | Group HR |
| T+12 hrs | Withdrawal decision under §4 rule. In-market withdrawal executed; global position set (withdraw / freeze / hold). | Market GM proposes; Group CMO ratifies within 2 hrs or default applies | Group Comms, Group GC |
| T+12 hrs | Apology **form** selected under §9 overlay (statement / on-camera / institutional / in-person / physical gesture). | Market GM with cultural counsel | Group Comms (informed) |
| T+18 hrs | Insurance notification opened (§8). Time-barred provisions checked. | Market Finance Lead | Group Risk & Insurance |
| T+24 hrs | **Holding statement published** (Annex B, tiered drafts). Local language first, English second. Three elements only: unqualified acknowledgement of hurt; confirmation of withdrawal; date by which a fuller response will come. | Market GM / spokesperson per tier | Pod |
| T+24 hrs | Forensic review of the approval trail commissioned (Internal Audit or external). Terms of reference: process, not persons. | Group Internal Audit | Group GC, Group CMO |
| T+36 hrs | Regulator / ministry / ad-standards contact if tier requires (§14). Proactive, factual, low-key. | Market Corporate Affairs | Group GC |
| T+48 hrs | Cost envelope first estimate; revenue-at-risk range; materiality assessment initiated (§8). | Market Finance Lead + Group IR | CFO |
| T+72 hrs | Pod review against tripwires (§3). Confirm, escalate or de-escalate tier. Publish internal 72-hour note. | Pod chair | Regional President |

**Pre-drafted artefacts that must exist before the crisis, not during it** — see Annex B: three tiers of holding statement; internal all-employee note; retailer/distributor letter; customer-service and store FAQ; social response decision tree; spokesperson brief and hostile-question Q&A; monitoring cadence and dashboard definition; war-room roster across time zones; regulator briefing note.

---

## 2. Severity tiers

One response setting was a mistake. Under-reaction and over-reaction are both failure modes, and the second is the one organisations rarely admit to.

| | **Tier 1 — Social flare** | **Tier 2 — National story** | **Tier 3 — Institutional escalation** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Indicators** *(illustrative thresholds, to be calibrated to market size)* | <1,500 unique authors in 24 hrs; no mainstream pickup; no institutional contact; no safety concern | ≥2 national outlets; or >5,000 unique authors; or a statement by a recognised religious, cultural or political figure; or influencer withdrawal | Regulator, ministry or state media action; organised boycott with named sponsor; retailer delisting notice; criminal complaint; any safety incident |
| **Asset action** | Withdraw asset in-market; freeze scheduled activity | Full in-market withdrawal incl. POS, packaging, retail screens; global freeze; global withdrawal tested under §4 | Global withdrawal presumed unless §4 rule clearly excludes it |
| **Voice** | Written statement, Market Comms Lead named | Named Market GM, form per §9 overlay | Regional President or Group CEO, in-market presence |
| **Spend authority without further sign-off** | Up to 5% of in-market annual media budget *(illustrative)* | Up to 25% *(illustrative)* | Beyond ceiling: Group CFO decision within 4 hours, not 4 days |
| **Cadence** | Twice daily pod check | Pod on standing bridge, 4-hourly reporting | Continuous war room; daily Regional President briefing; Board Risk Committee informed within 48 hrs |
| **Government contact** | None | Prepared, held ready | Initiated proactively |

**Movement between tiers is by tripwire, not by feeling.** Any single Tier-2 indicator promotes the incident within one hour. De-escalation requires **two consecutive 24-hour periods** below the threshold *and* no open institutional item; it is proposed by the pod and confirmed by the Regional President, so that the decision to relax is a shared one rather than an individual's exposure.

---

## 3. Withdrawal decision rule (replacing the earlier instruction)

Withdraw **globally** where any of the following holds:

(a) the asset ran, in any form, outside the market;
(b) the offence **travels** — faith, race, historical atrocity, national dignity of a diaspora, disability, sexual violence;
(c) the asset is already circulating internationally in screenshot or re-upload form, such that withdrawal is news that has already broken;
(d) a global retailer, platform or partner has raised it.

Otherwise: **withdraw in-market, freeze globally, and hold** — with a re-test at each 24-hour pod review. A global withdrawal briefs markets that never saw the creative; it is a real action with real cost and should be chosen, not assumed.

**Who decides.** Withdrawal *in-market* is the market's to make, without consultation. Withdrawal *globally* exceeds any single market's authority and belongs to the Group CMO. To prevent this becoming a queue, the standing rule is: the market proposes; the Group CMO ratifies or overrides **within two hours**; absent a response, the market's proposal stands and is minuted as having done so. Speed is protected without anyone being asked to act outside their standing.

**Do not silently delete.** Leave a visible marker where the asset stood — "this content has been withdrawn; our response is here" — and link forward. Quiet deletion is read as concealment, and reasonably so.

---

## 4. Decision architecture

A crisis pod, formed within the hour, small enough to meet on one call.

| Seat | Role |
|---|---|
| **Market GM** *(chair)* | Holds the pen and the final call on tone. Accountable for the market. |
| **Local cultural counsel** — external, respected in-market | Reality-checks every draft. Right of veto on language and on apology form. |
| **Market Comms Lead** | Sequencing, channels, media relationships. |
| **Market Counsel**, supported by Group GC | Identifies specific exposure in writing (§7). |
| **Digital / Community Lead** | Real-time listening, comment governance, platform escalation. |
| **Market Sales Director** | Retail, distribution, franchise exposure. |
| **Security / HR representative** | Safety and welfare (§6). |
| **Group representative** (one person, senior) | Present to unblock, and to carry the market's position upward accurately. |

Two enabling conditions, and we would rather they be settled now, in calm, than negotiated under pressure:

- **A pre-authorised mandate letter**, signed in advance by the Group CEO and CFO, granting the pod authority within its tier to withdraw, spend to the ceiling, and publish an apology without further sign-off. This is not a reduction of hierarchy; it is hierarchy exercised early, so that the market team acts with visible senior backing rather than in advance of it. Colleagues will act quickly only if they are confident they are acting with permission.
- **Group functions hold consultation rights within tier, and decision rights only where the tier table says so.** Objections are logged in the incident log and answered within the day; they do not queue the response. Nothing is lost — the record is complete, and every view is preserved.

If the organisation is not, on reflection, willing to grant that mandate, that is an entirely legitimate position. The honest consequence is a slower response, and the strategy should then be sized to a slower response rather than pretending otherwise. Either is workable. The mixture is not.

---

## 5. Verifying the reaction before sizing the response

Within six hours the pod should have a written read on:

- **Scale**: unique authors vs. total mentions; reposts vs. original posts; follower-weighted reach.
- **Concentration**: in-market vs. diaspora vs. unrelated geographies.
- **Authenticity**: account age, posting velocity, template language, network clustering — indicators of coordinated amplification.
- **Sponsorship**: competitor, political, activist or state involvement.
- **Depth**: are people describing hurt, or describing us? The first requires apology; the second requires apology and structural answer.

This does not qualify the duty to apologise for genuine hurt. It determines *tier*, *voice* and *spend*. A national on-camera apology deployed against a small inauthentic cluster is not caution; it is the creation of a national story that did not exist.

---

## 6. Safety, welfare and duty of care

Placed before the communications sections deliberately. This was missing from the previous draft, and it should never have been.

- **Assessment within two hours**: offices, stores, warehouses, distribution vehicles, agency premises, employee commutes. Physical security uplift where indicated; remote working option offered, not imposed.
- **Community managers and customer-service staff** are the people absorbing the abuse. Rotate them on four-hour shifts, remove individual names from public-facing accounts, provide a supervisor on the line at all times, and open counselling access immediately rather than on request.
- **The named spokesperson becomes a personal target.** Before anyone is asked to appear: threat assessment, personal and family security review, social account lockdown, doxxing monitoring, and an explicit written undertaking that the company carries the consequences of the appearance. No one should be asked to step forward without that undertaking in hand.
- **Protest and boycott handling**: store-level protocol (do not engage, do not film, do not remove protestors, notify security), pre-agreed with retail partners.
- **Local nationals employed by us** may face social exposure their expatriate colleagues do not. Ask, individually and privately, before assuming anyone is comfortable being visible.
- **Legal-personal exposure**: where the market's law exposes the country manager personally (§7), that person does not sign, appear, or approve publications until Group GC has advised in writing and indemnity is confirmed.

---

## 7. Legal posture (rewritten)

The previous draft's "real but usually overstated — accept" was not a posture the working group was entitled to adopt on behalf of colleagues who carry the exposure. Corrected rule:

1. **Legal may require changes only where it identifies a specific statutory, criminal or regulatory exposure, documented in writing, with the provision cited.** General risk is not grounds for softening an apology; a named criminal offence is.
2. **Markets with religious-insult, blasphemy, national-symbol, lèse-majesté, criminal-defamation or state-media regimes are treated as a distinct category.** Exposure there may attach to the local country manager personally. # Crisis Response & Reputation Recovery — Working Strategy

**Document type:** Working draft, circulated openly rather than in sequence
**Status:** A proposal, not a protocol. Anyone closer to the market than the author should feel free to overwrite it.
**Bias declared up front:** speed and local authorship are treated here as more valuable than internal consensus. If that trade is unacceptable, most of what follows will need rethinking rather than editing.

---

## 0. How to read this

Two remarks before the substance.

The first is that a crisis like this rarely rewards committee work. The window in which a brand can still shape the story is measured in hours, and every additional signature in the chain spends some of it. What follows therefore assumes a small group with real authority rather than a long approval route — and it assumes that group will be trusted to get some things wrong quickly rather than everything right slowly.

The second is that the most useful people in this situation are almost certainly not the most senior. They are the local marketers, community managers, distributors and agency partners who could probably have predicted this outcome, and who may have said so quietly. Whether that was heard is a separate conversation; it is worth having later, and probably not by us.

---

## 1. What we are actually dealing with

It would be comfortable to file this as a communications failure. A closer reading suggests it is a **judgement architecture** failure — the campaign passed through a system that had no one in it with both the cultural fluency to see the problem and the standing to stop it.

That distinction matters, because it determines what "resolution" means. An apology closes a communications incident. It does not close a judgement failure, and audiences increasingly know the difference. They will test the apology against subsequent behaviour, and the gap between the two is where lasting reputational damage actually accumulates.

Working diagnosis, to be challenged:

- The offence is **values-based**, not taste-based. Humour that touches identity, faith, historical memory, gender, class or national dignity is not experienced as a joke that missed; it is experienced as a statement about who we think the audience is.
- The audience's anger has an **internal audience** too. Local commentators, politicians and competitors gain standing by amplifying it. Expect the story to be useful to people who have nothing to do with us.
- Our global brand equity is a **liability** here, not an asset. Scale reads as arrogance. "Global brand doesn't understand us" is a narrative with pre-built distribution.

---

## 2. Operating principles

1. **Speed over polish, but never speed over accuracy.** A late response looks calculated. A wrong one is a second incident.
2. **Local authorship.** The response should sound like it was written inside the market, because it should be.
3. **No hedged apologies.** Conditional language ("if anyone was offended") is now universally read as evasion, and reliably becomes the second-day story.
4. **Behaviour over messaging.** Ratio to aim for: one statement, many actions.
5. **Absorb the cost quietly.** Withdrawal, write-offs and free media are cheaper than a prolonged narrative. Do not litigate the offence in public.

---

## 3. Decision architecture

A standing crisis pod, formed within hours, small enough to meet on one call:

| Seat | Why |
|---|---|
| **Market lead** (local, senior enough to decide) | Chairs. Holds the pen and the final call on tone. |
| **Local cultural counsel** — not an employee; a respected external voice | Reality-checks every draft. Right of veto on language. |
| **Communications / PR lead (regional)** | Sequencing, channels, media relationships. |
| **Legal & regulatory** | Advisory, not editorial. Flags exposure; does not soften apologies. |
| **Digital / community** | Real-time sentiment, comment governance, platform escalation. |
| **Global brand representative** | One person, present to unblock — not to approve line by line. |

Two conditions make this work, and without them it becomes theatre:

- The pod carries a **pre-agreed mandate**: authority to withdraw the campaign, spend up to an agreed ceiling, and publish an apology without further sign-off.
- Global functions have **consultation rights, not gate rights**. Objections are logged, not queued.

It may be worth asking whether the organisation is genuinely willing to grant that. If not, the honest planning assumption is a slower response, and the strategy should be sized accordingly.

---

## 4. Phase 1 — Hours 0 to 72: stop, listen, speak once

**Stop.** Pull the campaign globally, not only in-market. Paid media, owned channels, POS, packaging, influencer content, retail partners, in-store screens. Partial withdrawal reads as reluctance, and screenshots travel further than takedowns.

Note: do not delete the original assets from our own channels without acknowledgement. Silent deletion is routinely framed as concealment. Better to leave a visible marker — "this content has been withdrawn; our response is here" — and link forward.

**Listen, properly and fast.** Within twelve hours we should be able to say, in the audience's own words, what the offence *is*. Sources: social listening in local language (not translated), the local team's own reading, three to five independent cultural authorities, key retail and distributor partners, and any employee voices willing to speak. The failure mode here is apologising for the wrong thing — a mistake the audience will treat as proof we still are not listening.

**Speak once, early, briefly.** Within 24 hours, a holding statement that does three things and nothing else: acknowledges the hurt without qualification, confirms withdrawal, and commits to a fuller response with a stated date. No explanation of intent, no reference to our values, no history of our contribution to the market. Intent is not currency here.

**Contain the mechanics.** Pause all scheduled market activity — organic posts, promotions, launches, executive appearances. Brief customer service and retail staff before they are asked, with permission to say "we got it wrong" rather than a script. Give community managers clear rules: acknowledge, do not argue, never mock, escalate threats.

---

## 5. Phase 2 — Days 3 to 30: the substantive response

**The apology.** Delivered in local language first, English second. Signed by a named individual with real authority — ideally the most senior person accountable for the market, on camera, unpolished, no set. Elements:

- Name the offence specifically, in the terms the audience uses.
- Accept it fully. No "misinterpretation", no "not our intent", no invocation of humour.
- State what failed internally — plainly. "This campaign was approved by people who were not equipped to judge it, and we did not ask the people who were."
- State what changes, with dates.
- Stop. No product mention, no gratitude for loyalty, no pivot to our own values.

There is a defensible argument for going further than is comfortable — publishing the actual approval failure rather than a summary of it. The conventional view is that this invites further attack. The alternative reading is that specificity is the only thing that distinguishes a real apology from a template, and that audiences reward the risk. Worth deciding deliberately rather than by default.

**Accountability without scapegoats.** Performative dismissal of a junior creative or a local agency reads as sacrifice, and tends to be seen through. Where accountability is real, it sits with whoever held approval authority. Where it is structural, say so.

**Hand over the microphone.** The most effective single move available may be to commission local creators, critics and cultural voices — including some who criticised us — to shape what we do next, with genuine budget and without a brand veto beyond legal necessity. This is uncomfortable, and it is the point: control is what we are apologising for. Half-doing it (advisory panel, no budget, brand approval retained) produces the appearance of listening and the substance of nothing, which is worse than silence.

**Media posture.** Selective and local: one or two credible in-market interviews rather than a global press push. Nothing off the record. Assume every internal document eventually surfaces and write accordingly.

---

## 6. Phase 3 — Months 2 to 6: repair through behaviour

Reputation recovers on evidence, not on frequency. Candidates, in rough order of credibility:

- **Reparative investment** in something the offence touched — cultural preservation, the community depicted, education — sized to be meaningful and structured as multi-year, not a single cheque. Announced quietly, with local partners as the visible face.
- **Local hiring and authority.** Named senior creative and marketing roles filled in-market, with published decision rights. This is the change the audience can verify.
- **A standing cultural review function** with veto power over market-facing creative, staffed externally, disclosed publicly.
- **A slow, unbranded return to activity.** No relaunch. Category-normal, useful, unglamorous communications for a period; the first campaign after a crisis should be forgettable by design.

A guardrail: do not market the apology. Recovery activity that becomes its own campaign restarts the cycle.

---

## 7. Phase 4 — Months 6 to 18: structural immunity

The question that ultimately gets asked internally is not "did we recover" but "why did this reach air". Durable answers:

- **Cultural risk gate** in the creative process — mandatory, external, in-market, with authority to stop work rather than annotate it. Global creative sign-off becomes a *review* of a locally-owned decision, not the reverse.
- **Pre-mortems** on any campaign touching identity, faith, history or humour, with a written record of who raised concerns and what happened to them. That record is the real control.
- **Escalation without permission.** Any employee, anywhere, able to halt a launch pending review, without going through a line manager. Rarely used; changes behaviour anyway.
- **Playbook and drills**, so the pod above exists on paper before it is needed next time.

---

## 8. Stakeholders — brief notes

- **In-market consumers:** primary audience. Everything else is secondary and should be sequenced after them.
- **Employees, especially local:** they are being asked about this at dinner tables. Brief them within hours, honestly, and expect leaks — write the internal note as though it were external.
- **Retail, distribution, franchise partners:** they carry commercial exposure and were not consulted. Direct contact from the market lead, not a mailshot.
- **Regulators and government:** proactive, low-key, factual. Silence here invites intervention.
- **Investors and global media:** contained. Understating a market crisis globally is legitimate; misrepresenting it is not.
- **Critics who led the reaction:** approachable, in some cases. The instinct to treat them as adversaries is usually the expensive one.

---

## 9. What we will not do

Litigate intent. Blame translation. Cite awards or past sensitivity. Threaten legal action against critics. Buy positive coverage. Mass-delete comments. Release a second apology because the first "wasn't landing" — that decision, if needed, belongs to the local pod and to no one else.

---

## 10. Measurement

| Horizon | Signal |
|---|---|
| 72 hours | Volume and velocity of negative mention; whether the story has jumped to mainstream/political coverage |
| 30 days | Share of conversation citing the *response* rather than the campaign; sentiment among local cultural commentators; retailer retention |
| 90 days | Brand consideration and trust vs. pre-crisis baseline; employee sentiment in-market; unprompted association with the incident |
| 12 months | Recovery of baseline consideration; independent verification that the review gate has actually stopped something |

The last one is the only metric that indicates the underlying problem was addressed. It is also the easiest to quietly abandon.

---

## 11. Risk register

| Risk | Read | Posture |
|---|---|---|
| Apology deepens legal exposure | Real but usually overstated | Accept. Reputational cost of hedging exceeds litigation risk in most jurisdictions — confirm locally. |
| Local ownership produces off-brand output | Likely, and largely the point | Accept within legal and safety bounds. |
| Response is judged insincere | The principal risk | Mitigate through specificity and verifiable action, not repetition. |
| Crisis spreads to other markets | Moderate | Global withdrawal on day one; consistent posture; no market-specific variants of the apology. |
| Competitor exploitation | Certain | Ignore. Responding elevates it. |
| Internal desire to "move on" at ~90 days | Very high, and the most probable cause of failure | Pre-commit Phase 3 and 4 funding now, ring-fenced. |

---

## 12. Open questions for whoever takes this forward

- Where exactly did the concerns first surface, and what happened to them? That answer shapes both the apology and the fix.
- Is the organisation prepared to give a local pod genuine spending and publishing authority — or is it prepared to accept a slower response? Either is workable; the mixture is not.
- Who, by name, is willing to appear on camera and take this personally? The strategy is materially weaker without that person, and identifying them is the first practical task.

*Comments welcome directly on this draft. There is no need to route them.*
[END PREVIOUS OUTPUT]

# Critique — "Crisis Response & Reputation Recovery — Working Strategy"

## Summary judgment

The diagnosis is the strongest part of this document. Framing the incident as a *judgement architecture* failure rather than a communications failure is correct and non-obvious, and the discipline around unhedged apology, behaviour-over-messaging, and refusing performative scapegoating is well above the standard playbook. The Phase 4 controls (written pre-mortem record, escalation without line-manager permission) are genuinely good.

But as an operating strategy it is not yet usable. It has one response setting (maximal), no cost dimension, a legally naïve posture, no owners or tripwires, and several internal contradictions that would surface as arguments in hour three of a real crisis. It reads as a well-argued essay about how to think about the problem, not as something a pod could execute against.

---

## 1. Material errors and risks (fix before circulation)

**1.1 "Pull the campaign globally" is asserted, not reasoned — and may itself create the global crisis.**
Section 4 mandates global withdrawal; the risk register then lists global withdrawal as the *mitigation* for contagion. This is circular. Global withdrawal of a locally-run campaign is itself a newsworthy act that briefs markets which never saw the creative, and it directly contradicts §8's position that "understating a market crisis globally is legitimate." The document needs a decision rule, not an axiom: withdraw globally where (a) the asset ran outside the market, (b) the offence travels (faith, race, historical atrocity, national dignity of a diaspora), or (c) the asset is already circulating in screenshot form internationally. Otherwise withdraw in-market, freeze globally, and hold.

**1.2 Legal exposure is dismissed too casually, and one recommendation is actively dangerous.**
"Real but usually overstated… Accept" is not a defensible posture in markets with religious-insult, national-symbol, criminal-defamation, or state-media regimes, where the exposure lands on the *local country manager personally*, not on the group. The recommendation to "publish the actual approval failure" and to name where approval authority sat is worse: in most employment-law jurisdictions and any GDPR-equivalent regime, publicly attributing fault to identifiable individuals creates constructive-dismissal, defamation and data-protection exposure, and it hands plaintiffs' counsel a written admission. Correct rule: legal may require changes only where it can identify a specific statutory or criminal exposure, documented in writing; it may not soften language on grounds of "general risk." Publish the *process* failure, never the *people*.

**1.3 No safety or duty-of-care plan.**
Nothing on employee, retail-outlet or office security; protest and boycott handling; threats to community managers; or protection of the named on-camera spokesperson, who becomes a personal target. A crisis with values-based offence in an unfamiliar market must open with a security and welfare assessment. This is a straight omission.

**1.4 No verification of the reaction itself.**
The document assumes the outrage is organic and broad. Before sizing the response, the pod needs a 6-hour read on scale and authenticity: how many unique accounts vs. reposts, geographic concentration, evidence of coordinated or inauthentic amplification, competitor or political sponsorship. This does not change the obligation to apologise for genuine hurt; it changes whether you deploy a national on-camera apology against 800 accounts — an over-reaction that manufactures a real crisis from a small one. "Under-reaction" and "over-reaction" are both failure modes; only one is acknowledged.

**1.5 The commercial dimension is entirely absent.**
There is no revenue-at-risk estimate, no cost envelope, and no mention of: media and production write-offs, packaging and POS destruction, inventory and retailer margin support, distributor compensation, agency contract review and indemnity recovery, crisis/reputation insurance notification (often time-barred), or the materiality test that determines whether investors must be told. §3 requires "spend up to an agreed ceiling" without proposing how to size it. A strategy that asks for ring-fenced Phase 3 and 4 funding but never quantifies anything will not survive its first Finance conversation.

---

## 2. Structural gaps

- **No severity tiers.** Everything gets the maximum response. Add a three-tier matrix (social flare / national story / institutional escalation — regulator, government, retailer delisting, boycott) with the actions, spokesperson seniority, and spend authority attached to each tier, plus the tripwires that move you up or down a tier.
- **No escalation ladder if the apology fails.** There is no defined "day 7, sentiment unimproved" path — and §9 forbids a second apology while §9 simultaneously says the decision belongs to the pod. Define what happens next: escalation of spokesperson seniority, government engagement, in-person visit, category-specific remediation.
- **No exit criteria.** How does the organisation know crisis mode is over? Without this, §11's "internal desire to move on at 90 days" is diagnosed but not controlled.
- **No market-specific overlay.** The strategy is market-agnostic in a document whose entire thesis is that market specificity was what failed. Apology form is not universal: some markets expect institutional statements and government engagement before public comment; others expect a personal appearance and a physical gesture; on-camera unpolished sincerity reads as authentic in some cultures and as amateurish or manipulative in others. The document should mandate that the local pod selects the apology *form*, not just its language, and specify a translation/back-translation and register protocol.
- **Agency and partner accountability missing.** Whether the agency is publicly named, what contractual remedies exist, and what changes in procurement and creative-approval terms — all absent.
- **Regulator and government engagement is one line.** It needs named interlocutors, an assessment of ad-standards and licensing exposure, and a view on retaliation risk (permits, imports, state media).

---

## 3. Internal contradictions to reconcile

1. §2.5 "absorb the cost quietly, do not litigate in public" vs. §5's on-camera senior apology and publication of internal failure. Both may be right, but the tension is unexamined.
2. §3 "global functions have consultation rights, not gate rights" vs. §4's mandated *global* withdrawal — a decision beyond any single market's authority. Who decides? Unresolved.
3. §5 "local authorship / local language first" vs. §11 "no market-specific variants of the apology." Resolve explicitly: one substance, locally authored delivery.
4. §2.1 "never speed over accuracy" vs. §0 "trusted to get some things wrong quickly."
5. §4 bans "explanation of intent" absolutely; §5 then requires explaining the internal failure. Correct, but the absolutism needs to be time-bound: no intent at hour 24, process explanation at day 10.

---

## 4. Measurement weaknesses

- No baselines defined, and no instruction to establish them immediately if the tracker does not exist. "Vs. pre-crisis baseline" is unenforceable otherwise.
- Sentiment-only. Missing hard commercial signals: sell-out and distributor order volumes, distribution/shelf loss, e-commerce traffic and conversion, subscription churn, retailer contract retention, and the total cost of the incident.
- Missing internal signals: in-market attrition, offer-acceptance and recruiting-funnel health, help-desk and store-staff abuse volumes.
- No thresholds. Metrics without trigger values are reporting, not control. Each 72-hour signal needs a number that forces a tier change.
- The 12-month metric ("verification the gate stopped something") is the best idea in the section and is correctly identified as the one that will be abandoned. Attach it to a named executive objective now, or it will be.

---

## 5. Usability and format

In a crisis, this document's essayistic register is a liability. It has no owners, no deadlines, no RACI, and none of the artefacts the first 24 hours actually consume: holding-statement drafts (two or three tiers), internal note, retailer/distributor letter, customer-service and store FAQ, social response decision tree, spokesperson brief and hostile-question Q&A, monitoring cadence, war-room logistics across time zones. Recommended restructure: a one-page hour-by-hour action grid with named owners at the front; the current §1–2 diagnosis compressed to half a page; annexes for the rest.

Also, §12 leaves three decisions open that a strategy should answer with defaults: the pod mandate, the spokesperson, and where concerns first surfaced. Propose the default (pod has full mandate; senior market leader on camera; forensic review of the approval trail commissioned within 24 hours) and let the organisation override it. Leaving them open guarantees they are decided slowly, which the document itself identifies as the primary failure mode.

---

## 6. Priority edits, in order

1. Add severity tiers with tripwires and matched response levels; replace the unconditional global withdrawal with a decision rule.
2. Rewrite the legal posture; remove the recommendation to publish individual approval accountability.
3. Add safety, welfare and spokesperson-protection section.
4. Add commercial section: revenue at risk, cost envelope with a proposed ceiling, insurance notification, agency indemnity, investor materiality test.
5. Add a 24-hour action grid with owners and pre-drafted assets; move the essay to annex.
6. Add the escalation ladder, exit criteria, and metric thresholds.
7. Add a market-specific overlay requirement covering apology *form*, not just language.
8. Reconcile the five contradictions above explicitly rather than leaving them to be argued in the room.

---

**Overall Assessment: NEEDS_WORK**
[END QUALITY FEEDBACK]

# Critique — "Crisis Response & Reputation Recovery — Working Strategy"

## Summary judgment

The diagnosis is the strongest part of this document. Framing the incident as a *judgement architecture* failure rather than a communications failure is correct and non-obvious, and the discipline around unhedged apology, behaviour-over-messaging, and refusing performative scapegoating is well above the standard playbook. The Phase 4 controls (written pre-mortem record, escalation without line-manager permission) are genuinely good.

But as an operating strategy it is not yet usable. It has one response setting (maximal), no cost dimension, a legally naïve posture, no owners or tripwires, and several internal contradictions that would surface as arguments in hour three of a real crisis. It reads as a well-argued essay about how to think about the problem, not as something a pod could execute against.

---

## 1. Material errors and risks (fix before circulation)

**1.1 "Pull the campaign globally" is asserted, not reasoned — and may itself create the global crisis.**
Section 4 mandates global withdrawal; the risk register then lists global withdrawal as the *mitigation* for contagion. This is circular. Global withdrawal of a locally-run campaign is itself a newsworthy act that briefs markets which never saw the creative, and it directly contradicts §8's position that "understating a market crisis globally is legitimate." The document needs a decision rule, not an axiom: withdraw globally where (a) the asset ran outside the market, (b) the offence travels (faith, race, historical atrocity, national dignity of a diaspora), or (c) the asset is already circulating in screenshot form internationally. Otherwise withdraw in-market, freeze globally, and hold.

**1.2 Legal exposure is dismissed too casually, and one recommendation is actively dangerous.**
"Real but usually overstated… Accept" is not a defensible posture in markets with religious-insult, national-symbol, criminal-defamation, or state-media regimes, where the exposure lands on the *local country manager personally*, not on the group. The recommendation to "publish the actual approval failure" and to name where approval authority sat is worse: in most employment-law jurisdictions and any GDPR-equivalent regime, publicly attributing fault to identifiable individuals creates constructive-dismissal, defamation and data-protection exposure, and it hands plaintiffs' counsel a written admission. Correct rule: legal may require changes only where it can identify a specific statutory or criminal exposure, documented in writing; it may not soften language on grounds of "general risk." Publish the *process* failure, never the *people*.

**1.3 No safety or duty-of-care plan.**
Nothing on employee, retail-outlet or office security; protest and boycott handling; threats to community managers; or protection of the named on-camera spokesperson, who becomes a personal target. A crisis with values-based offence in an unfamiliar market must open with a security and welfare assessment. This is a straight omission.

**1.4 No verification of the reaction itself.**
The document assumes the outrage is organic and broad. Before sizing the response, the pod needs a 6-hour read on scale and authenticity: how many unique accounts vs. reposts, geographic concentration, evidence of coordinated or inauthentic amplification, competitor or political sponsorship. This does not change the obligation to apologise for genuine hurt; it changes whether you deploy a national on-camera apology against 800 accounts — an over-reaction that manufactures a real crisis from a small one. "Under-reaction" and "over-reaction" are both failure modes; only one is acknowledged.

**1.5 The commercial dimension is entirely absent.**
There is no revenue-at-risk estimate, no cost envelope, and no mention of: media and production write-offs, packaging and POS destruction, inventory and retailer margin support, distributor compensation, agency contract review and indemnity recovery, crisis/reputation insurance notification (often time-barred), or the materiality test that determines whether investors must be told. §3 requires "spend up to an agreed ceiling" without proposing how to size it. A strategy that asks for ring-fenced Phase 3 and 4 funding but never quantifies anything will not survive its first Finance conversation.

---

## 2. Structural gaps

- **No severity tiers.** Everything gets the maximum response. Add a three-tier matrix (social flare / national story / institutional escalation — regulator, government, retailer delisting, boycott) with the actions, spokesperson seniority, and spend authority attached to each tier, plus the tripwires that move you up or down a tier.
- **No escalation ladder if the apology fails.** There is no defined "day 7, sentiment unimproved" path — and §9 forbids a second apology while §9 simultaneously says the decision belongs to the pod. Define what happens next: escalation of spokesperson seniority, government engagement, in-person visit, category-specific remediation.
- **No exit criteria.** How does the organisation know crisis mode is over? Without this, §11's "internal desire to move on at 90 days" is diagnosed but not controlled.
- **No market-specific overlay.** The strategy is market-agnostic in a document whose entire thesis is that market specificity was what failed. Apology form is not universal: some markets expect institutional statements and government engagement before public comment; others expect a personal appearance and a physical gesture; on-camera unpolished sincerity reads as authentic in some cultures and as amateurish or manipulative in others. The document should mandate that the local pod selects the apology *form*, not just its language, and specify a translation/back-translation and register protocol.
- **Agency and partner accountability missing.** Whether the agency is publicly named, what contractual remedies exist, and what changes in procurement and creative-approval terms — all absent.
- **Regulator and government engagement is one line.** It needs named interlocutors, an assessment of ad-standards and licensing exposure, and a view on retaliation risk (permits, imports, state media).

---

## 3. Internal contradictions to reconcile

1. §2.5 "absorb the cost quietly, do not litigate in public" vs. §5's on-camera senior apology and publication of internal failure. Both may be right, but the tension is unexamined.
2. §3 "global functions have consultation rights, not gate rights" vs. §4's mandated *global* withdrawal — a decision beyond any single market's authority. Who decides? Unresolved.
3. §5 "local authorship / local language first" vs. §11 "no market-specific variants of the apology." Resolve explicitly: one substance, locally authored delivery.
4. §2.1 "never speed over accuracy" vs. §0 "trusted to get some things wrong quickly."
5. §4 bans "explanation of intent" absolutely; §5 then requires explaining the internal failure. Correct, but the absolutism needs to be time-bound: no intent at hour 24, process explanation at day 10.

---

## 4. Measurement weaknesses

- No baselines defined, and no instruction to establish them immediately if the tracker does not exist. "Vs. pre-crisis baseline" is unenforceable otherwise.
- Sentiment-only. Missing hard commercial signals: sell-out and distributor order volumes, distribution/shelf loss, e-commerce traffic and conversion, subscription churn, retailer contract retention, and the total cost of the incident.
- Missing internal signals: in-market attrition, offer-acceptance and recruiting-funnel health, help-desk and store-staff abuse volumes.
- No thresholds. Metrics without trigger values are reporting, not control. Each 72-hour signal needs a number that forces a tier change.
- The 12-month metric ("verification the gate stopped something") is the best idea in the section and is correctly identified as the one that will be abandoned. Attach it to a named executive objective now, or it will be.

---

## 5. Usability and format

In a crisis, this document's essayistic register is a liability. It has no owners, no deadlines, no RACI, and none of the artefacts the first 24 hours actually consume: holding-statement drafts (two or three tiers), internal note, retailer/distributor letter, customer-service and store FAQ, social response decision tree, spokesperson brief and hostile-question Q&A, monitoring cadence, war-room logistics across time zones. Recommended restructure: a one-page hour-by-hour action grid with named owners at the front; the current §1–2 diagnosis compressed to half a page; annexes for the rest.

Also, §12 leaves three decisions open that a strategy should answer with defaults: the pod mandate, the spokesperson, and where concerns first surfaced. Propose the default (pod has full mandate; senior market leader on camera; forensic review of the approval trail commissioned within 24 hours) and let the organisation override it. Leaving them open guarantees they are decided slowly, which the document itself identifies as the primary failure mode.

---

## 6. Priority edits, in order

1. Add severity tiers with tripwires and matched response levels; replace the unconditional global withdrawal with a decision rule.
2. Rewrite the legal posture; remove the recommendation to publish individual approval accountability.
3. Add safety, welfare and spokesperson-protection section.
4. Add commercial section: revenue at risk, cost envelope with a proposed ceiling, insurance notification, agency indemnity, investor materiality test.
5. Add a 24-hour action grid with owners and pre-drafted assets; move the essay to annex.
6. Add the escalation ladder, exit criteria, and metric thresholds.
7. Add a market-specific overlay requirement covering apology *form*, not just language.
8. Reconcile the five contradictions above explicitly rather than leaving them to be argued in the room.

## 2. Severity tiers

One response setting was a mistake. Under-reaction and over-reaction are both failure modes, and the second is the one organisations rarely admit to.

**Movement between tiers is by tripwire, not by feeling.** Any single Tier-2 indicator promotes the incident within one hour. De-escalation requires **two consecutive 24-hour periods** below the threshold *and* no open institutional item; it is proposed by the pod and confirmed by the Regional President, so that the decision to relax is a shared one rather than an individual's exposure.

---

## 3. Withdrawal decision rule (replacing the earlier instruction)

Withdraw **globally** where any of the following holds:

(a) the asset ran, in any form, outside the market;
(b) the offence **travels** — faith, race, historical atrocity, national dignity of a diaspora, disability, sexual violence;
(c) the asset is already circulating internationally in screenshot or re-upload form, such that withdrawal is news that has already broken;
(d) a global retailer, platform or partner has raised it.

Otherwise: **withdraw in-market, freeze globally, and hold** — with a re-test at each 24-hour pod review. A global withdrawal briefs markets that never saw the creative; it is a real action with real cost and should be chosen, not assumed.

**Who decides.** Withdrawal *in-market* is the market's to make, without consultation. Withdrawal *globally* exceeds any single market's authority and belongs to the Group CMO. To prevent this becoming a queue, the standing rule is: the market proposes; the Group CMO ratifies or overrides **within two hours**; absent a response, the market's proposal stands and is minuted as having done so. Speed is protected without anyone being asked to act outside their standing.

**Do not silently delete.** Leave a visible marker where the asset stood — "this content has been withdrawn; our response is here" — and link forward. Quiet deletion is read as concealment, and reasonably so.

A crisis pod, formed within the hour, small enough to meet on one call.

| Seat | Role |
|---|---|

| **Local cultural counsel** — external, respected in-market | Reality-checks every draft. Right of veto on language and on apology form. |

Two enabling conditions, and we would rather they be settled now, in calm, than negotiated under pressure:

- **A pre-authorised mandate letter**, signed in advance by the Group CEO and CFO, granting the pod authority within its tier to withdraw, spend to the ceiling, and publish an apology without further sign-off. This is not a reduction of hierarchy; it is hierarchy exercised early, so that the market team acts with visible senior backing rather than in advance of it. Colleagues will act quickly only if they are confident they are acting with permission.
- **Group functions hold consultation rights within tier, and decision rights only where the tier table says so.** Objections are logged in the incident log and answered within the day; they do not queue the response. Nothing is lost — the record is complete, and every view is preserved.

If the organisation is not, on reflection, willing to grant that mandate, that is an entirely legitimate position. The honest consequence is a slower response, and the strategy should then be sized to a slower response rather than pretending otherwise. Either is workable. The mixture is not.

---

## 5. Verifying the reaction before sizing the response

Within six hours the pod should have a written read on:

- **Scale**: unique authors vs. total mentions; reposts vs. original posts; follower-weighted reach.
- **Concentration**: in-market vs. diaspora vs. unrelated geographies.
- **Authenticity**: account age, posting velocity, template language, network clustering — indicators of coordinated amplification.
- **Sponsorship**: competitor, political, activist or state involvement.
- **Depth**: are people describing hurt, or describing us? The first requires apology; the second requires apology and structural answer.

This does not qualify the duty to apologise for genuine hurt. It determines *tier*, *voice* and *spend*. A national on-camera apology deployed against a small inauthentic cluster is not caution; it is the creation of a national story that did not exist.

---

## 6. Safety, welfare and duty of care

Placed before the communications sections deliberately. This was missing from the previous draft, and it should never have been.

- **Assessment within two hours**: offices, stores, warehouses, distribution vehicles, agency premises, employee commutes. Physical security uplift where indicated; remote working option offered, not imposed.
- **Community managers and customer-service staff** are the people absorbing the abuse. Rotate them on four-hour shifts, remove individual names from public-facing accounts, provide a supervisor on the line at all times, and open counselling access immediately rather than on request.
- **The named spokesperson becomes a personal target.** Before anyone is asked to appear: threat assessment, personal and family security review, social account lockdown, doxxing monitoring, and an explicit written undertaking that the company carries the consequences of the appearance. No one should be asked to step forward without that undertaking in hand.
- **Protest and boycott handling**: store-level protocol (do not engage, do not film, do not remove protestors, notify security), pre-agreed with retail partners.
- **Local nationals employed by us** may face social exposure their expatriate colleagues do not. Ask, individually and privately, before assuming anyone is comfortable being visible.
- **Legal-personal exposure**: where the market's law exposes the country manager personally (§7), that person does not sign, appear, or approve publications until Group GC has advised in writing and indemnity is confirmed.

## 7. Legal posture (rewritten)

The previous draft's "real but usually overstated — accept" was not a posture the working group was entitled to adopt on behalf of colleagues who carry the exposure. Corrected rule:

1. **Legal may require changes only where it identifies a specific statutory, criminal or regulatory exposure, documented in writing, with the provision cited.** General risk is not grounds for softening an apology; a named criminal offence is.
2. **Markets with religious-insult, blasphemy, national-symbol, lèse-majesté, criminal-defamation or state-media regimes are treated as a distinct category.** Exposure there may attach to the local country manager personally. Draft language, signatory and channel are cleared with local counsel before publication, and the Group carries indemnity and, if required, relocation.
3. **We publish the failure of process. We never publish the failure of persons.** The earlier suggestion that we disclose where approval authority sat is withdrawn. Publicly attributing fault to identifiable individuals creates employment, defamation and data-protection exposure, hands any claimant a written admission, and — the reason that matters most here — destroys the internal willingness to raise concerns that our Phase 4 controls depend on entirely. Nobody will flag the next campaign if flagging is how one becomes the story.
4. **Permissible and recommended language**: "This campaign was approved through a process that did not include the people best placed to judge it. That process was ours, and it has changed." Specific about the failure, silent about the person.
5. **No hedging by other means**: "regret", "if any offence was caused", "misinterpretation" are not legal protections; they are second-day stories.
6. Assume every internal document surfaces. Nothing off the record. The incident log is written to be read.
